# SpatialRegimeModels

## `ChowRegimeTest`

    ChowRegimeTest

Test of coefficient equality across regimes, returned by
[`regime_chow_test`](@ref).

Fields: `stat`, `df`, `p_value`, and the two log-likelihoods `ll_pooled`
and `ll_regime`. Failing to reject means the pooled model is adequate and
the regime split is not buying anything.

!!! note
    If the regimes came from [`skater_regimes`](@ref) rather than from
    outside knowledge, this p-value is optimistic: the split was chosen
    using the same data it is being tested on.

## `ExogenousRegimes`

    ExogenousRegimes(labels)

Regime membership supplied directly, as an integer label per unit.

Use this when the grouping is known in advance — states, planning regions,
pre- and post-reform periods. When it is not, [`skater_regimes`](@ref)
derives spatially contiguous regimes from the data instead.

### Examples
```julia
fit_spatial_regime(W, X, y, ExogenousRegimes(region_id))
```

## `SpatialRegimeModel`

    SpatialRegimeModel

A spatial regime model, returned by [`fit_spatial_regime`](@ref):
coefficients are allowed to differ across groups of units rather than being
held constant over the whole map.

A discrete alternative to GWR — where `fit_gwr` lets coefficients
vary smoothly with location, this estimates one set per regime, which is
easier to interpret and test when the groups are meaningful. Use
[`regime_chow_test`](@ref) to ask whether the split is warranted.

## `fit_spatial_regime`

    fit_spatial_regime(W, X, y, regimes; spatial_lag=true, varnames=nothing, method=ChebyshevApprox(),
                       rho_bounds=(-0.995, 0.995))

Fit a spatial regime model where coefficients vary across regimes:
  y = ρWy + X_r β_r + ε   (spatial_lag=true)
  y = X_r β_r + ε          (spatial_lag=false)

Each regime gets its own intercept and slope coefficients.
Anselin (1988, 1990).

!!! note "Identification"
    The design has to have full column rank. `X` goes in without an
    intercept, since one is added, and no covariate may be a linear
    combination of the others. A design that fails this throws an
    `ArgumentError` naming the offending column, rather than failing
    inside the linear algebra or returning an arbitrary split of one
    coefficient across two.

    The design is block diagonal in the regimes, so a covariate that is
    constant inside one regime collides with that regime's intercept even
    when it varies across the sample as a whole.

`rho_bounds` is the search interval for `ρ`, as in
[`fit_spatial`](@ref SpatialEconometrics.SpatialEconometricsPrototype.fit_spatial).

## `regime_chow_test`

    regime_chow_test(pooled_model, regime_model)

Likelihood ratio test for structural stability across spatial regimes.
H₀: coefficients are equal across all regimes.

## `skater_regimes`

    skater_regimes(W, X, n_regimes; min_size=1, rng=Random.default_rng())

Spatially constrained clustering via SKATER minimum spanning tree partitioning.
Returns an `ExogenousRegimes` assignment with `n_regimes` contiguous groups, each
guaranteed to be a connected region of `W`.

A minimum spanning tree is built over the contiguity graph with edge weights given
by Euclidean distance between the standardised rows of `X`. The tree is then split
`n_regimes - 1` times, each time choosing the edge whose removal most reduces the
within-group sum of squared deviations.

`min_size` is the smallest admissible region; cuts that would leave a smaller
component are skipped. Raise it when the regions feed a regime regression, which
needs enough units per region to identify its own coefficients.

Assunção et al. (2006) "Efficient regionalization techniques for socio‐economic
geographical units using minimum spanning trees."
